tip: In orario is a fixed phrase meaning on time; keep in with no article.
Singular family members skip the article with possessives: mia moglie, not la mia moglie.
Feminine una shortens to un' before a vowel: un'amica. Masculine un takes no apostrophe.
Dito is irregular: one is il dito, but several become le dita, switching to feminine plural.
Da means from: da qui is from here, so lontano da qui asks the distance from here.
Dire has the irregular past participle detto: hai detto means you said, never hai dicuto.

english: Can you show me the way?
tip: An object pronoun attaches to the end of an infinitive: indicare plus mi becomes indicarmi.

english: Can you explain it to me?
tip: Before another pronoun, mi changes to me: me lo puoi spiegare is can you explain it to me.
After a preposition, tu becomes te: orgoglioso di te, never di tu.
Negatives come in pairs: non plus mai means never, and both words are kept: non sta fermo mai.
To ask whose, Italian uses di chi, literally of whom: di chi è questo libro.
Nascere takes essere in the past: sono nato is literally 'I am born'. The participle nato agrees with the subject.
With essere the participle agrees with the subject: sei nata ends in -a because the 'you' is female; a man would say sei nato.
Su plus il merges into one word, sul: sul letto means on the bed.

english: What time do you wake up?
tip: Svegliarsi ends in -si, so it needs a matching pronoun: ti svegli = you wake up. The 'self' is not literal in English.

english: It's too hot in here, isn't it?
tip: Weather uses fare, not essere: fa caldo means it's hot, and fa freddo means it's cold.
Nascere, to be born, forms its past with essere: è nato means he was born.
Countries take in with no article: in Italia, in Francia. È nata in Italia is born in Italy.

english: Does this train go to Milan?
tip: Cities take a, not in: va a Milano means goes to Milan.

english: The girlfriends go out for dinner.
tip: Amica adds an h in the plural to keep the hard c sound: amica becomes amiche.

target: L'elettricista ha controllato l'impianto della cucina.
english: The electrician checked the kitchen wiring.
tip: Nouns ending in -ista are the same for men and women; only the article shows gender: l'elettricista.
Subject pronouns are usually dropped, so adding noi adds emphasis: noi siamo ottimisti stresses 'we'. Plain siamo ottimisti is enough.
The accent on è marks the verb, meaning is, from essere. Without it, e just means and: È tutto chiaro.
Piacere works backwards: the liked thing is the subject. Ti piace l'Italia = literally 'Italy is pleasing to you'.
Perché does double duty: it asks 'why' in a question and means 'because' in the answer. Perché sei triste = why are you sad.
Reflexive verbs stick their pronoun onto the infinitive: sedersi becomes sedermi, to seat myself, after posso.
Essere is the helper here and the participle agrees: a man is sei stato, a woman is sei stata.
With avere as the helper, the past participle stays fixed: hai studiato never changes for gender.
Collegarsi is reflexive, so the mi stays: mi collego means I connect myself, here to a network.
Here ci means each other: ci incontriamo is we meet one another, not just we meet.
